analysis.one_liner: Requires drug patent owners to prove each patent covers a distinct invention or surrender patent rights after the first expires.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by a Democrat with Republican cosponsors, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and its courts subcommittee in June 2019 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drug companies often list many patents on a single medicine. Each patent can last a different length of time, so as one expires the company can rely on the next to keep cheaper generic or biosimilar copies off the market — a practice that stretches one invention into decades of monopoly pricing. This bill would flip the burden: a patent owner listing multiple patents on one drug would have to prove each one covers a genuinely different invention, or else patent protection for all of them ends when the first patent expires. That rule would apply both to court cases challenging the patents and to lawsuits drug companies file against generic and biosimilar makers seeking FDA approval. It would also direct the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office to review whether its own procedures let drug makers obtain overlapping patents, and report to Congress within a year [S2, S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take brand-name drugs would benefit from earlier generic and biosimilar competition, which typically brings prices down sharply. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers would also benefit, because they would face fewer overlapping patent lawsuits used to delay FDA approval of their copies [S2, S3].

how_it_helps.text: In any proceeding challenging a drug's listed patents, or in an infringement suit against a company seeking FDA approval for a generic or biosimilar, the patent owner must prove each listed patent covers a patentably distinct invention. If it cannot, the patents are treated as disclaimed after the first one expires [S2, S3].
This targets the practice of stacking multiple patents on one drug so that exclusivity lasts far longer than the original patent, which keeps lower-priced copies off the market [S2].

The bill also directs the Patent Office to comprehensively review whether its examination procedures improperly allow multiple non-distinct patents on the same drug, and to report findings and recommendations to the House Judiciary Committee within one year [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would lose the ability to extend a drug's monopoly with overlapping patents on the same invention, reducing the extra years of high-price sales those patent stacks currently protect [S2, S3].

drawbacks.text: Patent owners would bear the burden of proving, in every challenge or infringement suit, that each listed patent is a distinct invention — a added litigation cost and uncertainty that could reach legitimate patents on genuine improvements to drugs [S2, S3].

Critics of anti-evergreening measures generally argue that weakening follow-on patents reduces the incentive to invest in improvements to existing medicines; this bill's presumption approach makes it harder, rather than easier, for a company to defend such patents.
The USPTO portion of the bill is only a study and a report; it would not itself change any examination procedure [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit of earlier generic competition is large, since stacked patents are a documented way drug monopolies outlast their intended terms. The main cost falls on drug companies, and the strongest honest objection is that the burden-shifting presumption could sweep in some legitimate improvement patents. On balance the bill is a targeted consumer-protection measure rather than a broad weakening of the patent system, but it never advanced far enough to be tested or amended.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its courts and intellectual property subcommittee, and sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Hakeem Jeffries introduced the bill on June 11, 2019, joined by Reps. Doug Collins of Georgia, Debbie Mucarsel-Powell, and Ben Cline, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1, S3, S5].
On June 28, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Courts, Intellectual Property, and the Internet — the last action ever taken on the bill [S5].

The bill accumulated 5 cosponsors, 3 Republicans and 2 Democrats, but the Judiciary Committee never reported it and the full House never voted on it before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1, S4, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off, because the overlapping patent protection this bill would have limited remains fully intact and they face no new burden of proving patent distinctness in court. Patients and generic makers gained nothing.

for.name: Hakeem Jeffries
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor

against.name: Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: Committee under his chairmanship took no action on the bill beyond referring it to a subcommittee; no markup or floor consideration was ever scheduled

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Democrat and the bill's cosponsors split 3 Republicans and 2 Democrats, so the bill's failure was not a party-line vote — it simply never reached one.

industries.note: The bill would end the practice of stacking multiple patents on one drug to extend exclusivity after the original patent expires. That extension is what keeps cheaper generic and biosimilar copies off the market and keeps drug prices high, so the industry's interest here runs directly against patients' interests [S2, S3].

The bill would limit the patent-infringement suits brand-name companies file against firms seeking FDA approval for copies, letting generics and biosimilars reach the market sooner. What is good for these companies in this case is also good for the patients who buy their lower-priced drugs [S2].
